Saturday. Ramesh had been getting five "hot tips" a week and felt more confused each time. He took a sheet and started writing rules for himself: small amounts, the same day every month; only products that are registered and regulated; nothing that promises a fixed high return. Vikas read it over his shoulder.

Wednesday. A colleague pitched a "guaranteed" scheme. Ramesh checked the sheet, saw the third rule, and said no in half a minute without arguing.

Sunday. The rules were stuck on the inside of the cupboard door. Ramesh said, "I no longer judge every pitch. The sheet does that." For personal choices Ramesh still planned to ask a qualified adviser.

passage:
Asif, you keep forwarding me these 'sure-shot' tips. Let me, Karthik, the boring one in this office, tell you how I stopped reading them.
With my first salary, I got a pitch every week. A chit scheme, a friend's 'guaranteed' plan, a man selling plots. Each time I had to decide on the spot, and each time I felt stupid and pressured.
So one Sunday I wrote my own rules on a single page and kept it in my wallet. One: small amounts, every month, same day. Two: only products a regulator watches, the ordinary kind, spread across many companies. Three: anything that promises a fixed high return, I don't even discuss.
After that, pitches got easy. A man at a wedding told me about 'eighteen percent assured'. I didn't have to think. Rule three. I smiled, ate my payasam and changed the subject.
So, Asif, write your page first. Then stop forwarding me things.

qa.q: What was rule three on Karthik's page?
qa.a: Anything that promises a fixed high return, Karthik doesn't even discuss.

qa.q: How did young Karthik feel deciding on each pitch on the spot?
qa.a: Stupid and pressured, having to judge every offer in the moment with nothing to guide the choice.

qa.q: What turning point in the story made the pitches easy, and why?
qa.a: Writing the one-page rules on a Sunday; with the decision made in advance, the wedding pitch needed no thought.

qa.q: How might the man at the wedding have seen young Karthik's reaction?
qa.a: Probably as polite but impossible to persuade, since the pitch never got a real hearing.

grounding: Shows a person writing a short personal investing policy in advance so each pitch no longer has to be judged in the moment.

Pradeep's phone had rung four times since breakfast: the same 'wealth manager' from a firm he'd never heard of, each time with a new product that 'closes Friday'. By lunch he couldn't think.
In the noisy hostel mess, Bidisha pushed a paper napkin at him. 'Stop deciding each one. Decide once.'
So he wrote a policy on the napkin, half shouting over the clatter of steel plates. 'One: ₹1,000 a month, on the 5th, no more for now. Two: only regulated products, the plain kind that hold lots of companies. Three: if anyone promises a fixed high return, I say no without discussing it.'
'And the calls?'
'Rule four: I never buy anything on a phone call.'
The fifth call came during dessert. Pradeep listened for ten seconds, heard 'guaranteed twenty percent', said, 'Not for me, thank you,' and hung up. He felt oddly light. The napkin went into his wallet.

qa.q: How much did Pradeep decide to put in each month?
How did Pradeep feel after hanging up on the fifth call?
qa.a: Oddly light and relieved, because the rules made the decision before the pressure could.

qa.q: What else could Pradeep add to the napkin policy?
qa.a: When to review the amount, and a trusted adult or registered adviser to ask before changing any rule.

qa.q: How does the situation look to Bidisha?
qa.a: Bidisha sees Pradeep worn out by the calls and offers a simple fix: decide once instead of every time.

grounding: Shows a person writing a short investing policy of small regular amounts in regulated products and no fixed high returns, so pitches are easy to refuse.
